To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in a mouse model of PyV infection and kidney transplantation, local virus-induced inflammation/infection is necessary to drive an augmented alloimmune response, which results in PyV associated allograft injury.
the primary antiviral immune system is not required for the induction of graft injury and that the primary alloimmune system is required for the induction graft injury.

the interplay between viral and alloimmune responses in a mouse model of PyV-associated kidney injury is complex, with the local virus-mediated inflammation/injury within grafts being a key determinant of allograft outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the immune system responds to viral infection and the impact of this on allograft injury.
the interplay between viral immunity and allogeneic immune responses.
how viral infections can influence allograft rejection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
local virus-associated inflammation and injury within allografts can alter host alloimmunity and promote allograft rejection in this mouse model.
the virus-induced injury within the graft is the primary driver of the alloimmune response and not the other way around.
the virus-induced inflammation/injuries are required to promote the alloimmune response and that the virus-induced inflammatory/injury alone is insufficient to promote allograft loss.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
local but not distant virus-induced inflammation and injury within an allograft is required for PyV-associated allogen-specific T cell activation.
the local virus-associated inflammation in the allograft is the primary driver for the alloimmune response.
the predominant mechanism of injury in PyV is an augmented alloimmune response due to virus-induced inflammation/injuy within the allograft.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the virus itself is not directly responsible for graft injury, but that the virus-induced inflammation/infection is responsible for the alloimmune response that is responsible for graft injury.
local virus-associated inflammation and injury within a graft are sufficient to promote allograft injury.
the virus-induced inflammatory response within the allograft is the primary driver of the alloimmune T cell responses.
